In this corpus, traditional support lookup tasks and structured BI-style questions differ primarily in query modality, data architecture, and output purpose.

Traditional support lookup tasks involve employees asking natural language questions to retrieve specific facts, policies, or procedures from unstructured document repositories. These are served through TutorChat's semantic query processing, vector search, and grounded answer generation with inline citations [NL-002#NL-002-S03]. Examples include specific policy queries like "What is our reimbursement limit for business meals in Canada?" or procedural queries like "What is the checklist for onboarding a new Enterprise customer?" [NL-028#NL-028-S06]. These tasks emphasize retrieving exact, verifiable text chunks, and their performance is evaluated via the Golden Dataset, which includes 40% "direct lookup" queries [NL-008#NL-008-S08].

Structured BI-style questions, by contrast, target relational database tables (e.g., the `support_tickets` table) and require programmatic SQL aggregations, groupings, and filters for analytical insights. The corpus explicitly provides SQL targets for these, such as `SELECT category, SUM(ticket_count) ... GROUP BY category` or `SELECT segment, AVG(ticket_count) ... GROUP BY segment` [NL-029#NL-029-S07]. These are used for operational audits and trend tracking—for example, extracting high-priority tickets active for more than 48 hours to identify SLA bottlenecks, or averaging CSAT scores across subscription plan tiers to target accounts before renewal [NL-029#NL-029-S07]. Unlike lookup tasks, which synthesize grounded answers from unstructured chunks, BI-style questions compute aggregate metrics and trends from structured data.

The key distinctions are: lookup tasks use natural-language semantic search over document chunks with inline citations [NL-002#NL-002-S03], while BI questions use deterministic SQL queries against structured tables for numerical aggregation and cross-referencing trends [NL-029#NL-029-S07]. The Golden Dataset also separates direct lookup (40%) from cross-document synthesis (30%), implying the latter represents more complex analytical or BI-style work [NL-008#NL-008-S08].
